summary: This memo describes IBM's support of Data Link Switching over TCP/IP, a way to carry traffic from IBM SNA and NetBIOS networks across an IP network. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1795.

plainLanguage.summary: Some older company networks could not speak Internet language. This paper describes a way to wrap their messages so they can travel across the Internet.

questions: how does dlsw carry sna over tcp
what is the switch to switch protocol
subtitle: How IBM carried SNA and NetBIOS traffic between routers over TCP by ending the data link at each switch.

tldr.problem: SNA and NetBIOS use LLC Type 2, which assumes small, predictable delay, so bridging it over slow, variable wide area links causes time-outs, extra acknowledgments and eventually dropped links.
tldr.mechanism: Data Link Switching terminates the LLC connection at each switch and multiplexes the connections over a TCP connection between switches, using the Switch-to-Switch Protocol (SSP) with a per-circuit state machine.
tldr.outcome: LLC time-outs and acknowledgments stay on the local LAN and TCP guarantees delivery between switches. The memo describes IBM's design for the IBM 6611 and was replaced by RFC 1795.

today: RFC 1434 is an Informational memo describing IBM's design and was obsoleted by RFC 1795, which is the document to read for the later version of Data Link Switching.

sections.title: What Data Link Switching Does
sections.content:
Data Link Switching (DLS) is a forwarding mechanism for the IBM SNA and IBM NetBIOS protocols. It does not provide full routing. It switches at the Data Link layer and encapsulates traffic in TCP/IP. The memo documents the Switch-to-Switch Protocol (SSP) used between IBM 6611 Network Processors, which support SNA (PU 2 and PU 4) and NetBIOS systems on token-ring networks, and SNA (PU 2) systems on SDLC links.

SNA and NetBIOS use IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) Type 2, which uses a fixed timer to detect lost frames. Over a wide area link the delay is larger and varies, so a delayed frame can trigger a retransmission that confuses LLC and eventually takes the link down. DLS addresses DLC time-outs, DLC acknowledgments over the WAN, flow and congestion control, broadcast control of search packets and source-route bridging hop count limits.
sections.plainLanguage: The old systems expect an answer very fast, like a friend next door. Over a long distance answers are slow, so they give up. DLS lets them talk to a nearby helper instead.

sections.title: Switching Versus Bridging
sections.content:
In traditional bridging the Data Link Control is end-to-end. In DLS, the switch terminates the LLC Type 2 connection, so LLC connections never cross the wide area network and the connection at each end is independent. The switch multiplexes LLC connections onto a TCP connection to another switch, and TCP guarantees delivery of frames between the switches.

As a result LLC time-outs stay on the local LAN, LLC acknowledgments (RRs) do not cross the WAN, SDLC polling happens locally, search frame broadcasts are controlled once a target is found, and switches can apply back pressure to end systems for flow and congestion control.

A single DLS can also switch one data link to another internally without TCP. A pair of switches uses SSP over a reliable transport. The first implementation uses TCP, although the memo says other transports such as OSI TP4 could be used. The default TCP parameters are socket family AF_INET, socket type SOCK_STREAM, read port number 2065 and write port number 2067.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending every little thank-you note across the ocean, each side talks to a local helper, and the two helpers keep a reliable line open between them.

sections.title: SSP Headers, Addresses and Message Types
sections.content:
SSP has two headers. The control message header is 72 bytes and is used for all messages except information messages. The information message header is 16 bytes and is identical to the first sixteen bytes of the control header. In the control header the Version Number is x'4B' (75), the Header Length is x'00 48' (72 bytes), the Header Number is x'01' and the Protocol ID is x'42' (66). Frame Direction is x'01' from origin to target and x'02' from target to origin. Reserved fields are set to zero on transmission and should be ignored on receipt.

A Data Link ID is 14 bytes: a pair of attachment addresses, each a 6 byte MAC address plus a 1 byte LLC address (link SAP). A Circuit ID is 64 bits (8 bytes), made of a 4 byte DLC Port ID and a 4 byte Data Link Correlator, assigned locally and unique within one switch. A pair of Circuit IDs plus the switch identifiers identifies one end-to-end circuit.

Table 1 of the memo lists 17 message types, such as CANUREACH (x'03'), ICANREACH (x'04'), CONTACT (x'08') and INFOFRAME (x'0A'). Values not listed are reserved. The NetBIOS control messages carry the entire DLC header, with the routing information field padded to 18 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has a label that says who it is from, who it is for and what kind it is. Short messages for ordinary data get a small label, and control messages get a bigger one.

sections.title: Setting Up, Restarting and Closing Circuits
sections.content:
To connect, an SNA origin station sends a Test command. The origin switch sends CANUREACH to the target switch, or to all remote switches if the target is unknown. The target switch sends its own Test command, and when the station answers it returns ICANREACH. If several switches can reach the target, the origin selects the first reply and sends REACH_ACK. Both switches are then in the circuit established state, where LLC Type 1 frames such as XID can flow. When the origin station sends a SABME command, CONTACT and CONTACTED messages set up the LLC Type 2 connection. NetBIOS systems follow a similar flow using Name Query and Name Recognized frames and the NETBIOS_NQ and NETBIOS_NR messages.

To restart, a SABME received during an active connection leads to a RESTART_DL message, a DISC to the target station and a DL_RESTARTED reply. To disconnect, a DISC from an end station leads to HALT_DL and DL_HALTED. If the TCP connection between switches fails, all connections multiplexed on it are taken down and DISC commands go to the local systems.

Each switch is assumed to build topology tables of which switches can reach a given MAC address or NetBIOS name, which keeps search traffic to a minimum.
sections.plainLanguage: First the helpers ask around to find the other computer, then they agree to open a line, and at the end they politely hang up together.

sections.title: The DLS State Machine
sections.content:
The protocol is defined by one state machine per end-to-end circuit, with eleven states. The initial state is DISCONNECTED. The steady states are DISCONNECTED, CIRCUIT_ESTABLISHED, where LLC Type 1 services are available end-to-end, and CONNECTED, where LLC Type 2 services are available too. The other eight are transitional: RESOLVE_PENDING, CIRCUIT_PENDING, CONNECT_PENDING, CONTACT_PENDING, CIRCUIT_RESTART, DISCONNECT_PENDING, HALT_PENDING and RESTART_PENDING.

Transitions depend on SSP messages and on local signals between the switch and its Data Link Control (DLC) entity, such as DLC_CONTACTED or DLC_ERROR. If an event is not listed for a state, no action and no state change occurs. The number of circuits a switch supports is a local implementation option. The memo adds notes where the IBM 6611 does something platform specific, such as sending a Test command to start a data link.

For NetBIOS datagrams, the memo gives tables showing how UI frames map onto SSP messages. For example, an add-name query sent to a group address becomes NETBIOS_ANQ sent to all remote switches.
sections.plainLanguage: Each conversation is like a traffic light with a few stages: nothing yet, path found, fully talking. The rules say which signal moves you to the next stage.
